question: What is HTML and what does it stand for?
options: HyperText Markup Language, a language for creating web pages
Hyperlink Transfer Machine, a protocol for data transfer
Home Tool Markup Language, a desktop application
HyperText Modeling Language, a database schema
correctAnswer: HyperText Markup Language, a language for creating web pages
explanation: HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language and is used to structure content on the web.

question: What is the difference between HTML elements and HTML tags?
options: Elements are the complete units including start tag, content, and end tag, while tags are only the opening or closing markup
Elements are only the opening tags, tags are the closing tags
Elements refer to CSS, tags refer to JavaScript
There is no difference; they are synonyms
correctAnswer: Elements are the complete units including start tag, content, and end tag, while tags are only the opening or closing markup
explanation: An element consists of a start tag, optional content, and an end tag; a tag is just the markup itself.

question: What is the basic structure of an HTML document?
options: <!DOCTYPE html>\\n<html>\\n<head>\\n<title>Title</title>\\n</head>\\n<body>\\n...content...\\n</body>\\n</html>
<html>\\n<head>\\n<title>Title</title>\\n</head>\\n<body>\\n...content...\\n</html>
<!DOCTYPE html>\\n<head>\\n<title>Title</title>\\n</head>\\n<body>\\n...content...\\n</body>

<html>
<body>
...content...
</body>
</html>
correctAnswer: <!DOCTYPE html>\\n<html>\\n<head>\\n<title>Title</title>\\n</head>\\n<body>\\n...content...\\n</body>\\n</html>
explanation: A valid HTML document starts with the DOCTYPE, then html, head (with title), and body sections.

question: What is the difference between block-level and inline elements in HTML?
options: Block-level elements start on a new line and take the full width, while inline elements flow within a line and only take the width of their content
Block-level elements can only contain text, while inline elements can contain other elements
Block-level elements are deprecated, inline elements are modern
Both types behave the same; the terms are interchangeable
correctAnswer: Block-level elements start on a new line and take the full width, while inline elements flow within a line and only take the width of their content
explanation:
Block-level elements create a new block (e.g.,
,

), whereas inline elements (e.g., , ) sit within a line of text.

question: What are semantic HTML elements? Give examples.
options: Elements that clearly describe their meaning to both browser and developer, such as <header>, <nav>, <article>, <section>, <footer>
Elements that add visual styling, like <b>, <i>, <u>, <font>
Elements that are only used for scripting, like <script> and <noscript>
Elements that are deprecated in HTML5, such as <center> and <font>
correctAnswer: Elements that clearly describe their meaning to both browser and developer, such as <header>, <nav>, <article>, <section>, <footer>
explanation: Semantic elements convey the purpose of the content, improving accessibility and SEO.

question: What is the purpose of the <!DOCTYPE html> declaration?
options: It tells the browser which version of HTML the page is written in.
It defines the character encoding of the document.
It links an external stylesheet to the page.
It creates a comment that is ignored by browsers.
correctAnswer: It tells the browser which version of HTML the page is written in.
explanation: The doctype informs the browser about the HTML version and triggers standards mode rendering.

question: What is the difference between <div> and <span>?
options: <div> is an inline element, while <span> is a block-level element.
<div> can contain only text, whereas <span> can contain other HTML elements.
<div> is a block-level element used for layout, while <span> is an inline element used for styling small pieces of text.
<div> automatically adds a line break, while <span> does not.
correctAnswer: <div> is a block-level element used for layout, while <span> is an inline element used for styling small pieces of text.
explanation: <div> creates a block container affecting layout, whereas <span> is inline and typically used for styling fragments of text.

question: What are HTML attributes and how are they used?
options: They are tags that define the structure of a page, used only in the <head> section.
They are name‑value pairs added to HTML tags to provide additional information or configure behavior.
They are CSS rules that style HTML elements.
They are JavaScript functions embedded inside HTML elements.
correctAnswer: They are name‑value pairs added to HTML tags to provide additional information or configure behavior.
explanation: Attributes appear inside start tags (e.g., <a href="...">) and modify the element's behavior or provide metadata.

question: What is the difference between HTML and XHTML?
options: HTML is case‑insensitive and allows omitted tags; XHTML is XML‑based, case‑sensitive, and requires well‑formed markup.
HTML uses .xhtml file extension while XHTML uses .html.
HTML supports multimedia, XHTML does not.
HTML is only for web pages, XHTML is for mobile apps.
correctAnswer: HTML is case‑insensitive and allows omitted tags; XHTML is XML‑based, case‑sensitive, and requires well‑formed markup.
explanation: XHTML follows XML rules, requiring proper nesting, closing tags, and case sensitivity, unlike traditional HTML.

question: What is the purpose of the <head> tag and what can it contain?
options: It displays the main content of the page and can contain paragraphs and images.
It defines the footer of the document and contains navigation links.
It contains meta-information about the document such as title, meta tags, links to stylesheets, and scripts; it is not displayed in the page body.
It is used to embed video content directly into the page.
correctAnswer: It contains meta-information about the document such as title, meta tags, links to stylesheets, and scripts; it is not displayed in the page body.
explanation: The <head> section holds metadata, title, links to CSS, scripts, and other information that does not render as page content.

question: What is the difference between <meta> tags used for charset and viewport?
options: Charset defines the character encoding of the document, while viewport controls the layout on mobile devices
Charset sets the page language, while viewport sets the page title
Charset defines CSS styles, while viewport defines JavaScript behavior
Both tags serve the same purpose
correctAnswer: Charset defines the character encoding of the document, while viewport controls the layout on mobile devices
explanation: The charset meta tag tells the browser which character set to use (e.g., UTF-8), whereas the viewport meta tag tells the browser how to scale and display the page on different screen sizes.

question: What is the difference between an ordered list and an unordered list?
options: An ordered list (<ol>) displays items with numbers, while an unordered list (<ul>) displays items with bullet points
An ordered list is used only for navigation menus, while an unordered list is used only for forms
An ordered list cannot contain nested lists, but an unordered list can
An ordered list is styled with CSS only, while an unordered list requires JavaScript
correctAnswer: An ordered list (<ol>) displays items with numbers, while an unordered list (<ul>) displays items with bullet points
explanation: <ol> creates a numbered list, indicating a specific order, whereas <ul> creates a bulleted list where order is not implied.

question: What is the difference between <a> href and <a> target attributes?
options: href specifies the URL the link points to, while target specifies where the linked document will open
href sets the link text, while target sets the link color
href defines a CSS class for the link, while target defines a JavaScript function to run
Both attributes are deprecated in HTML5
correctAnswer: href specifies the URL the link points to, while target specifies where the linked document will open
explanation: The href attribute contains the destination URL, and the target attribute determines the browsing context (e.g., _blank opens in a new tab).

question: What is the purpose of the alt attribute on an tag?
options: It provides alternative text for accessibility and when the image cannot be displayed
It sets the image border thickness
It defines the image file size
It controls the animation speed of the image
correctAnswer: It provides alternative text for accessibility and when the image cannot be displayed
explanation: The alt attribute supplies descriptive text that screen readers can read and that appears if the image fails to load, improving accessibility.

question: What is the difference between HTML entities and regular characters?
options: Entities represent characters that would otherwise be interpreted as markup, using the &...; syntax
Entities are used only in CSS stylesheets
Regular characters cannot be displayed in HTML documents
Entities are only used for emoji characters
correctAnswer: Entities represent characters that would otherwise be interpreted as markup, using the &...; syntax
explanation: HTML entities (e.g., &, <) allow you to display characters like < or & that have special meaning in HTML markup.

question: What is the difference between id and class attributes in HTML?
options: An id must be unique within a page, while a class can be used on multiple elements.
An id can be used on multiple elements, while a class must be unique.
Both id and class must be unique.
Both id and class can be used on any number of elements.
correctAnswer: An id must be unique within a page, while a class can be used on multiple elements.
explanation: The id attribute is required to be unique in the document, whereas the class attribute can be applied to many elements for shared styling or behavior.

question: What are HTML data attributes and how are they used?
options: Custom attributes prefixed with "data-" that store private data for the page and can be accessed via JavaScript.
Standard attributes that define the visual style of an element.
Attributes that replace the need for CSS.
Deprecated attributes removed in HTML5.
correctAnswer: Custom attributes prefixed with "data-" that store private data for the page and can be accessed via JavaScript.
explanation: Data attributes allow developers to embed custom data in HTML elements; they start with "data-" and are accessible through the DOM (e.g., element.dataset).

question: What is the difference between <section>, <article>, and <div>?
options: <section> defines a thematic grouping, <article> defines a self-contained composition, and <div> is a generic container with no semantic meaning.
<section> is for navigation, <article> for footers, <div> for headers.
All three are identical and interchangeable.
<div> provides semantic meaning while <section> and <article> do not.
correctAnswer: <section> defines a thematic grouping, <article> defines a self-contained composition, and <div> is a generic container with no semantic meaning.
explanation: <section> groups related content, <article> represents an independent piece that could be syndicated, and <div> is a non-semantic block-level element used for styling or scripting.

question: What is the difference between <header>, <footer>, <nav>, and <aside>?
options: <header> defines introductory content, <footer> defines footer content, <nav> defines navigation links, and <aside> defines tangentially related content.
<header> is for navigation, <footer> for sidebars, <nav> for headers, <aside> for footers.
All four are generic containers without semantic meaning.
<aside> is used for main content, while the others are for decorative purposes.
correctAnswer: <header> defines introductory content, <footer> defines footer content, <nav> defines navigation links, and <aside> defines tangentially related content.
explanation: Each element provides specific semantic meaning: <header> for introductory material, <footer> for concluding material, <nav> for navigation blocks, and <aside> for content related to the main flow but not central.

question: What is the purpose of the <figure> and <figcaption> elements?
options: <figure> groups self-contained media content, and <figcaption> provides a caption or legend for that content.
<figure> creates a table, and <figcaption> adds a header row.
<figure> is used for form inputs, and <figcaption> validates them.
correctAnswer: <figure> groups self-contained media content, and <figcaption> provides a caption or legend for that content.
explanation: <figure> is used to encapsulate media such as images, diagrams, or code snippets, and <figcaption> supplies a descriptive caption associated with that figure.

question: What is the difference between <b>/<strong> and <i>/<em>?
options: <b> provides visual bold styling while <strong> conveys semantic importance; <i> provides visual italic styling while <em> conveys semantic emphasis.
All four tags are deprecated in HTML5 and should not be used.
<b> and <i> add CSS classes automatically, whereas <strong> and <em> trigger JavaScript events.
There is no difference; they are exact synonyms.
correctAnswer: <b> provides visual bold styling while <strong> conveys semantic importance; <i> provides visual italic styling while <em> conveys semantic emphasis.
explanation: <b> and <i> are presentational tags, while <strong> and <em> add meaning (importance and emphasis) in addition to default styling.

question: What is a void element in HTML? Give examples.
options:
Elements that cannot have any content and are self‑closing, such as ,
,
, and .
Elements that must contain a <script> child element.

Elements that require an explicit closing tag like
or

.
Elements that are only valid in HTML5 and not in earlier versions.
correctAnswer:
Elements that cannot have any content and are self‑closing, such as ,
,
, and .
explanation: Void elements are defined by the HTML specification as having no end tag and no content; they are written as self‑closing tags.

question: What is the difference between HTML5 and HTML4?
options: HTML5 adds new semantic elements, multimedia tags, and APIs that HTML4 lacks.
HTML5 removes support for tables entirely, which HTML4 provides.
HTML4 uses strict XML syntax while HTML5 does not.
HTML5 is designed only for mobile browsers, whereas HTML4 is for desktop browsers.
correctAnswer: HTML5 adds new semantic elements, multimedia tags, and APIs that HTML4 lacks.
explanation: HTML5 introduces elements like <section>, <article>, <video>, <audio>, and many new APIs, expanding capabilities beyond HTML4.

question: What is the purpose of the lang attribute on the <html> tag?
options: It specifies the primary language of the document for accessibility tools, search engines, and translation services.
It sets the default font family for the entire page.
It determines the character encoding (e.g., UTF‑8).
It enables or disables JavaScript execution for the page.
correctAnswer: It specifies the primary language of the document for accessibility tools, search engines, and translation services.
explanation: The lang attribute informs browsers and assistive technologies about the document's language, aiding pronunciation, indexing, and translation.

question: What is the difference between absolute, relative, and root‑relative URLs in HTML links?
options: An absolute URL includes the full scheme and domain; a relative URL is based on the current document’s path; a root‑relative URL starts with '/' and is resolved from the site root.
Absolute URLs are used only for images, relative URLs only for scripts, and root‑relative URLs only for CSS files.
Absolute URLs are always shorter than relative URLs, and root‑relative URLs are identical to absolute URLs.
There is no functional difference; the three terms are interchangeable.
correctAnswer: An absolute URL includes the full scheme and domain; a relative URL is based on the current document’s path; a root‑relative URL starts with '/' and is resolved from the site root.
explanation: These three URL forms determine how the browser resolves the link: absolute includes protocol and host, relative depends on the current location, and root‑relative starts from the domain root.

question: What is the difference between <script> placed in the head vs at the end of the body?
options: When placed in the head, the script blocks HTML parsing until it is downloaded and executed; when placed at the end of the body, the HTML is parsed first, so the page renders faster.
Scripts in the head are executed after the page loads, while scripts at the end run before any content is displayed.
Head scripts are only for external files, body scripts must be inline.
There is no difference; browsers treat them the same.
correctAnswer: When placed in the head, the script blocks HTML parsing until it is downloaded and executed; when placed at the end of the body, the HTML is parsed first, so the page renders faster.
explanation: A script in the head blocks parsing and rendering until it finishes, whereas placing it just before </body> lets the browser render the page first and then execute the script, improving perceived load speed.

question: What is the difference between async and defer attributes on a <script> tag?
options: async downloads the script asynchronously and executes it as soon as it is ready, possibly before HTML parsing finishes; defer downloads asynchronously but executes only after the HTML document has been fully parsed.
async executes after defer, both block rendering.
Both async and defer guarantee execution order as they appear in the document.
async works only with external scripts, defer works only with inline scripts.
correctAnswer: async downloads the script asynchronously and executes it as soon as it is ready, possibly before HTML parsing finishes; defer downloads asynchronously but executes only after the HTML document has been fully parsed.
explanation: async runs the script immediately when it finishes downloading, which can interrupt parsing; defer waits until parsing is complete, preserving document order.

question: What is the difference between <link> and <script> tags in terms of resource loading?
options: <link> is used to load external resources like stylesheets and is fetched in parallel without blocking rendering, while <script> loads JavaScript and can block rendering unless async/defer are used.
<link> loads JavaScript, <script> loads CSS.
Both tags load resources synchronously and block rendering.
Only <script> can load external files; <link> is only for internal resources.
correctAnswer: <link> is used to load external resources like stylesheets and is fetched in parallel without blocking rendering, while <script> loads JavaScript and can block rendering unless async/defer are used.
explanation: <link> typically loads CSS, which the browser can fetch in parallel and apply after download, while <script> loads JavaScript that may halt parsing unless its loading behavior is altered with async or defer.

question: What is the purpose of the <base> tag in HTML?
options: It sets the base URL for all relative URLs in the document and optionally the default target for hyperlinks and forms.
It defines the base font size for the page.
It creates a base element for CSS inheritance.
It is used to embed a base64-encoded image.
correctAnswer: It sets the base URL for all relative URLs in the document and optionally the default target for hyperlinks and forms.
explanation: The <base> element establishes a reference URL that the browser uses to resolve any relative links or form actions, and can also set a default target window.

question: What is an HTML form and what is it used for?
options: An HTML form is a container for input controls that allows users to submit data to a server for processing.
An HTML form is a way to style text with CSS.
An HTML form is a script that runs on page load.
An HTML form is used to embed multimedia content.
correctAnswer: An HTML form is a container for input controls that allows users to submit data to a server for processing.
explanation: Forms group input elements (text fields, buttons, etc.) and send the collected data to a server endpoint via GET or POST when the user submits the form.

question: What is the difference between GET and POST methods in an HTML form?
options: GET appends form data to the URL and is limited in length; POST sends data in the request body and has no size limit.
GET encrypts the data while POST does not.
GET can only be used for submitting forms, POST cannot.
GET uses HTTP/2 and POST uses HTTP/1.1.
correctAnswer: GET appends form data to the URL and is limited in length; POST sends data in the request body and has no size limit.
explanation: GET includes the data in the query string of the URL, which is visible and length‑limited; POST sends the data in the request body, keeping it out of the URL and allowing larger payloads.

question: What is the difference between <input type='text'> and <textarea>?
options: <input type='text'> creates a single-line text field; <textarea> creates a multi-line text area.
<input type='text'> supports rich text formatting; <textarea> does not.
<input type='text'> can upload files; <textarea> cannot.
<input type='text'> is only for numbers; <textarea> is for dates.
correctAnswer: <input type='text'> creates a single-line text field; <textarea> creates a multi-line text area.
explanation: The <input> element with type='text' renders a single‑line input box, whereas <textarea> provides a larger, multi‑line area for longer text.

question: What are the different input types introduced in HTML5?
options: email, url, number, date, range, color, tel, search, datetime-local, month, week, time
text, password, hidden, button, submit, reset
file, image, hidden, password
radio, checkbox, select, option
correctAnswer: email, url, number, date, range, color, tel, search, datetime-local, month, week, time
explanation: HTML5 added many new input types such as email, url, number, date, range, color, tel, search, datetime-local, month, week, and time to improve native validation and UI controls.

question: What is the purpose of the required, pattern, and placeholder attributes in form inputs?
options: required forces a field to be filled; pattern defines a regex the input must match; placeholder shows example text inside the field.
required encrypts the data; pattern sets the field's background color; placeholder disables the field.
required makes the field read‑only; pattern changes the input type; placeholder submits the form automatically.
required adds a tooltip; pattern validates the form on the server; placeholder sets the field's name attribute.
correctAnswer: required forces a field to be filled; pattern defines a regex the input must match; placeholder shows example text inside the field.
explanation: 'required' makes the field mandatory, 'pattern' provides a regular‑expression constraint, and 'placeholder' displays hint text that disappears when the user types.

question: What is the difference between a <select> element and a <datalist> element?
options: <select> provides a dropdown list of predefined options that must be chosen; <datalist> offers autocomplete suggestions while still allowing free text entry.
<select> allows multiple selections by default; <datalist> does not support multiple selections.
<select> is only for numeric values; <datalist> is only for dates.
<select> requires JavaScript to function; <datalist> works without any HTML.
correctAnswer: <select> provides a dropdown list of predefined options that must be chosen; <datalist> offers autocomplete suggestions while still allowing free text entry.
explanation: The <select> element restricts input to its listed options, whereas <datalist> supplies suggested values but lets the user type any value.

question: What is form validation and how does HTML5 support native validation?
options: Form validation checks user input on the server side only; HTML5 provides no native validation features.
Form validation ensures that user input meets specified criteria; HTML5 adds built-in attributes like required, pattern, type, minlength, etc., that perform client‑side validation automatically.
Form validation is the process of encrypting form data; HTML5 supports it via the <encrypt> tag.
Form validation refers to styling forms with CSS; HTML5 supports it through the <style> attribute.
correctAnswer: Form validation ensures that user input meets specified criteria; HTML5 adds built-in attributes like required, pattern, type, minlength, etc., that perform client‑side validation automatically.
explanation: HTML5 introduces attributes such as required, pattern, type, minlength, maxlength, etc., which let browsers validate inputs on the client without extra JavaScript.

question: What is the difference between <button type='submit'> and <button type='button'>?
options: <button type='submit'> triggers form submission; <button type='button'> does nothing unless scripted.
<button type='submit'> creates a new form; <button type='button'> deletes the form.
<button type='submit'> is only for GET method; <button type='button'> is only for POST.
<button type='submit'> disables the form; <button type='button'> enables it.
correctAnswer: <button type='submit'> triggers form submission; <button type='button'> does nothing unless scripted.
explanation: A submit button automatically sends the form data to the action URL, while a button of type 'button' has no default behavior and must be handled with script.

question: What is the purpose of the <fieldset> and <legend> elements?
options: <fieldset> groups related controls; <legend> provides a caption for the group.
<fieldset> creates a table; <legend> adds a tooltip.
<fieldset> validates inputs; <legend> disables them.
<fieldset> is for styling only; <legend> is for scripting.
correctAnswer: <fieldset> groups related controls; <legend> provides a caption for the group.
explanation: <fieldset> semantically groups form controls, and <legend> gives that group a visible title, improving accessibility and organization.

question: What is the difference between disabled and readonly attributes on form inputs?
options: disabled prevents the control from being focused or submitted; readonly allows focus but prevents editing while still submitting its value.
disabled makes the control invisible; readonly hides its label.
disabled works only on buttons; readonly works only on text inputs.
disabled and readonly are synonyms.
correctAnswer: disabled prevents the control from being focused or submitted; readonly allows focus but prevents editing while still submitting its value.
explanation: A disabled field is excluded from form submission and cannot receive focus; a readonly field can be focused and its value is sent, but the user cannot modify it.

question: What is the purpose of the name attribute on form inputs and how is it used on submission?
options: The name attribute identifies the control's data key; upon submission the name/value pair is sent to the server.
The name attribute sets the visible label of the input.
The name attribute determines the input's CSS class.
The name attribute encrypts the input value.
correctAnswer: The name attribute identifies the control's data key; upon submission the name/value pair is sent to the server.
explanation: When a form is submitted, each input's name becomes the key in the query string or request body, paired with its current value, allowing the server to process the data.

question: What is the purpose of <thead>, <tbody>, and <tfoot> in a table?
options: They define header, body, and footer rows for styling and accessibility.
They are used to create separate tables.
They are deprecated.
They automatically sort table data.
correctAnswer: They define header, body, and footer rows for styling and accessibility.
explanation: Thead, tbody, and tfoot group rows semantically, aiding styling, accessibility, and scripts.

question: What is the difference between the <video> and <audio> elements?
options: <video> displays video, <audio> displays audio.
<video> only works in Chrome, <audio> works in all browsers.
<video> requires a source tag, <audio> does not.
<video> is for images, <audio> is for sound.
correctAnswer: <video> displays video, <audio> displays audio.
explanation: <video> embeds video content; <audio> embeds audio-only content.

question: What are the common attributes used with the <video> tag (controls, autoplay, loop, muted)?
options: controls, autoplay, loop, muted
src, width, height, poster
alt, title, class, id
data, role, aria-label, tabindex
correctAnswer: controls, autoplay, loop, muted
explanation: These attributes control playback UI, auto‑play, looping, and mute state.

question: What is the purpose of the <source> element inside <video> or <audio>?
options: To provide multiple media formats for browser compatibility.
To set the volume level.
To display captions.
To embed subtitles.
correctAnswer: To provide multiple media formats for browser compatibility.
explanation: <source> lets the browser pick the first supported format, ensuring compatibility.

question: What is the difference between , , and for responsive images?
options: displays a single image, allows multiple sources for different media queries, is used within to specify each source.
is for video, is for audio, is for text.
is deprecated, is new, is obsolete.
All three are identical.
correctAnswer: displays a single image, allows multiple sources for different media queries, is used within to specify each source.
explanation: <picture> with <source> lets browsers choose the best image based on media queries or type.

question: What is the srcset attribute used for in responsive images?
options: Specify multiple image sources for different resolutions
Set the source of an image element
Define the alt text
Control image caching
correctAnswer: Specify multiple image sources for different resolutions
explanation: The srcset attribute lets the browser choose the most appropriate image based on device pixel density, viewport size, or other criteria, enabling responsive image delivery.

question: What is the difference between SVG and Canvas for rendering graphics in HTML?
options: SVG is vector-based and DOM-accessible, Canvas is pixel-based and imperative
SVG is raster and Canvas is vector
Both are vector but SVG is older
Canvas is only for 3D
correctAnswer: SVG is vector-based and DOM-accessible, Canvas is pixel-based and imperative
explanation: SVG creates scalable vector graphics that are part of the DOM and can be styled or scripted, while Canvas draws pixels on a bitmap and is manipulated imperatively via JavaScript.

question: What is the difference between localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies?
options: localStorage persists across sessions, sessionStorage lasts per tab, cookies are sent to server
localStorage is server-side, sessionStorage is client-side, cookies are database
localStorage is for images, sessionStorage for text, cookies for audio
All are the same but have different names
correctAnswer: localStorage persists across sessions, sessionStorage lasts per tab, cookies are sent to server
explanation: localStorage data remains until cleared, sessionStorage data is cleared when the tab closes, and cookies are included with every HTTP request to the server.

question: What is the size limitation of localStorage compared to cookies?
options: localStorage ~5MB, cookies ~4KB
localStorage ~4KB, cookies ~5MB
Both ~5MB
localStorage unlimited, cookies limited
correctAnswer: localStorage ~5MB, cookies ~4KB
explanation: Browsers typically allow about 5 megabytes per origin for localStorage, whereas each cookie is limited to roughly 4 kilobytes.

question: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous storage APIs (e.g., localStorage vs IndexedDB)?
options: localStorage is synchronous and blocks the main thread, IndexedDB is asynchronous and non-blocking
localStorage is async, IndexedDB is sync
Both are sync
Both are async
correctAnswer: localStorage is synchronous and blocks the main thread, IndexedDB is asynchronous and non-blocking
explanation: localStorage operations execute immediately and can freeze the UI, while IndexedDB uses callbacks or promises to perform operations without blocking the main thread.

question: What is IndexedDB and when would you use it over localStorage?
options: IndexedDB is a synchronous key-value store that stores only strings.
IndexedDB is an asynchronous object store that can store structured data and large amounts of data.
IndexedDB is limited to 5MB of storage per domain.
IndexedDB is only available in Internet Explorer.
correctAnswer: IndexedDB is an asynchronous object store that can store structured data and large amounts of data.
explanation: IndexedDB supports complex data types, larger storage limits, and asynchronous access, making it preferable over localStorage for large or structured data.

question: What is the purpose of the HttpOnly and Secure flags on cookies?
options: HttpOnly prevents client‑side scripts from accessing the cookie, and Secure ensures the cookie is only sent over HTTPS.
HttpOnly allows cross‑site requests, and Secure allows the cookie to be sent over HTTP.
HttpOnly encrypts the cookie value, and Secure sets the cookie to be HTTP only.
HttpOnly and Secure are the same flag and both restrict cookie usage to the same domain.
correctAnswer: HttpOnly prevents client‑side scripts from accessing the cookie, and Secure ensures the cookie is only sent over HTTPS.
explanation: HttpOnly blocks JavaScript access, mitigating XSS, while Secure forces HTTPS transmission, protecting the cookie from being sent over insecure connections.

question: What is the SameSite attribute on cookies and why was it introduced?
options: It controls whether a cookie is sent with cross‑site requests, introduced to mitigate CSRF attacks.
It determines the expiration time of a cookie.
It specifies the domain that can read the cookie.
SameSite is a feature for session storage only.
correctAnswer: It controls whether a cookie is sent with cross‑site requests, introduced to mitigate CSRF attacks.
explanation: SameSite limits cookie transmission to same-site contexts, reducing the risk of cross‑site request forgery.

question: What is the Cache API and how is it used with Service Workers?
options: It allows storing network responses for offline use and is accessed by Service Workers to intercept fetch events.
It is a server‑side caching mechanism for database queries.
It replaces localStorage for all client‑side data storage.
It is only used for caching images in the browser.
correctAnswer: It allows storing network responses for offline use and is accessed by Service Workers to intercept fetch events.
explanation: The Cache API provides a key‑value store of Request/Response objects that Service Workers can read/write during fetch handling, enabling offline functionality.

question: What are Service Workers and how do they enable offline functionality?
options: Background scripts that intercept network requests, allowing the app to serve cached assets when offline.
They are only used for push notifications.
They are part of HTML5 form validation.
They are used to render CSS stylesheets.
correctAnswer: Background scripts that intercept network requests, allowing the app to serve cached assets when offline.
explanation: Service Workers run separately from the main thread, intercept fetch events, and can serve cached responses, enabling the application to function without a network connection.

question: What is a Progressive Web App (PWA) and what HTML/browser features enable it?
options: A native app built with HTML, CSS, and JS that runs offline using Service Workers and Web App Manifest.
A web page that uses AJAX to load content dynamically.
A website that uses Flash for animations.
A server-side rendered application.
correctAnswer: A native app built with HTML, CSS, and JS that runs offline using Service Workers and Web App Manifest.
explanation: PWAs are web apps that feel native, using Service Workers for offline caching, a Web App Manifest for installability, and modern APIs to provide a native‑like experience.

question: What is the difference between the History API (pushState) and traditional page navigation?
options: pushState changes the URL without reloading the page, while traditional navigation reloads the page.
pushState loads a new page from the server, traditional navigation updates the DOM.
pushState is only for mobile browsers, traditional navigation is for desktop.
pushState is a CSS feature.
correctAnswer: pushState changes the URL without reloading the page, while traditional navigation reloads the page.
explanation: The History API lets scripts modify the browser history and URL without triggering a full page load, enabling single‑page‑app navigation.

question: What is the HTML Canvas element used for?
options: Rendering raster graphics via JavaScript.
Defining semantic sections of a page.
Embedding videos.
Creating forms.
correctAnswer: Rendering raster graphics via JavaScript.
explanation: The <canvas> element provides a bitmap surface that JavaScript can draw on, ideal for games, charts, and other dynamic graphics.

question: What is the difference between the 2D context and WebGL context on a canvas?
options: 2D context uses CPU for rendering, WebGL uses GPU for 3D.
2D context is for text only, WebGL is for images.
2D context is deprecated, WebGL is the new standard.
They are the same.
correctAnswer: 2D context uses CPU for rendering, WebGL uses GPU for 3D.
explanation: The 2D context draws 2‑D shapes using CPU, while WebGL taps the GPU for accelerated 3‑D rendering.

question: How does the Canvas API differ from SVG in terms of performance and use cases?
options: Canvas is pixel-based and faster for animations, SVG is vector-based and better for static graphics.
Canvas is vector-based and better for static graphics, SVG is pixel-based.
Canvas cannot be styled with CSS, SVG can.
Canvas is only for 3D.
correctAnswer: Canvas is pixel-based and faster for animations, SVG is vector-based and better for static graphics.
explanation: Canvas draws pixels directly, making it efficient for frequent redraws like games, whereas SVG keeps a DOM of shapes, excelling at scalable, interactive graphics.

question: What is an SVG element and how is it embedded in HTML?
options: It is a vector graphics format that can be included using the <svg> tag directly in HTML.
It is a raster image format that requires the tag.
It is a script element for animations.
It is a CSS property.
correctAnswer: It is a vector graphics format that can be included using the <svg> tag directly in HTML.
explanation: SVG is an XML-based vector graphics format that can be embedded inline with the <svg> element in HTML.

question: What is the viewBox attribute in SVG used for?
options: It defines the coordinate system and scaling of the SVG content.
It specifies the background color of the SVG.
It sets the width and height of the SVG element.
It controls the animation timing of the SVG.
correctAnswer: It defines the coordinate system and scaling of the SVG content.
explanation: The viewBox attribute establishes the internal coordinate system and how the SVG scales to fit its container.

question: How would you animate elements drawn on an HTML canvas?
options: By using requestAnimationFrame to redraw frames in a loop.
By applying CSS transitions to the canvas element.
By using the <animate> tag inside the canvas.
By setting the 'animation' attribute on the canvas.
correctAnswer: By using requestAnimationFrame to redraw frames in a loop.
explanation: Canvas animations require repeatedly drawing frames, typically done with requestAnimationFrame for smooth performance.

question: What are ARIA attributes in HTML and why are they important for accessibility?
options: They provide semantic information to assistive technologies, improving accessibility.
They are used to style elements with CSS.
They define the layout of the page.
They are only for debugging.
correctAnswer: They provide semantic information to assistive technologies, improving accessibility.
explanation: ARIA attributes give screen readers context about elements that lack native semantics, enhancing accessibility.

question: What is the difference between aria-label and aria-labelledby?
options: aria-label provides a text label, while aria-labelledby references another element's text.
aria-label is for images, aria-labelledby is for forms.
aria-label is deprecated, aria-labelledby is current.
They are identical.
correctAnswer: aria-label provides a text label, while aria-labelledby references another element's text.
explanation: aria-label supplies an explicit label string, whereas aria-labelledby points to an existing element whose text becomes the accessible name.

question: What is the role attribute in ARIA and how is it used?
options: It defines the CSS role of an element.
It specifies the semantic role of an element for assistive technology.
It sets the JavaScript event handler for an element.
It controls the element's visibility on the page.
correctAnswer: It specifies the semantic role of an element for assistive technology.
explanation: The ARIA role attribute tells assistive technologies what kind of widget or landmark an element represents.

question: What is the tabindex attribute and how does it affect keyboard navigation?
options: It sets the tab order and can be negative to remove an element from the tab order.
It changes the font size of the element.
It defines the color theme of the element.
It controls the scrolling behavior of the page.
correctAnswer: It sets the tab order and can be negative to remove an element from the tab order.
explanation: tabindex determines the order in which elements receive focus when the user presses the Tab key, and a negative value excludes the element from the tab sequence.

question: What is the purpose of the alt attribute for screen readers, and when should it be left empty?
options: It provides an image description; leave it empty for decorative images.
It sets alt text for CSS styling purposes.
It determines the file path of the image.
It has no effect on accessibility.
correctAnswer: It provides an image description; leave it empty for decorative images.
explanation: alt text conveys the meaning of an image to screen readers; it should be omitted (empty) when the image is purely decorative.

question: What is the accessibility tree and how does the browser construct it from the DOM?
options: It is a tree of CSS styles applied to elements.
It is a tree of DOM nodes with ARIA roles, built by filtering the DOM and merging ARIA attributes.
It is a tree of JavaScript objects representing event listeners.
It is a tree of network requests made by the page.
correctAnswer: It is a tree of DOM nodes with ARIA roles, built by filtering the DOM and merging ARIA attributes.
explanation: The browser creates an accessibility tree by traversing the DOM, applying ARIA roles and properties, and discarding non‑accessible nodes.

question: What is the difference between accessible and semantic markup?
options: Accessible markup uses ARIA; semantic markup uses proper HTML tags.
Semantic markup is always accessible.
Accessible markup is only for screen readers.
There is no difference between the two.
correctAnswer: Accessible markup uses ARIA; semantic markup uses proper HTML tags.
explanation: Semantic markup relies on native HTML elements that convey meaning, while accessible markup adds ARIA attributes to improve assistive‑technology support.

question: What is HTML template element (<template>) and how does it differ from regular hidden content?
options: It is a container for reusable content that is not rendered until instantiated.
It is a hidden element that is rendered but not visible.
It is a script tag that runs JavaScript.
It is a CSS class that hides content.
correctAnswer: It is a container for reusable content that is not rendered until instantiated.
explanation: The <template> element holds inert DOM that is not rendered until activated via JavaScript, unlike regular hidden content which is still part of the layout.

question: What is the difference between Web Workers and Service Workers?
options: Web Workers run in background threads for CPU tasks; Service Workers intercept network requests and cache responses.
Web Workers are for caching; Service Workers are for UI updates.
Web Workers are only for images; Service Workers only for audio.
Both are identical.
correctAnswer: Web Workers run in background threads for CPU tasks; Service Workers intercept network requests and cache responses.
explanation: Web Workers provide parallel execution of scripts; Service Workers act as a network proxy to cache and serve resources.

question: How does preloading resources with <link rel='preload'> affect page load performance?
options: It tells the browser to fetch the resource early, reducing latency for critical assets.
It delays the download until after the page loads.
It only works for CSS files.
It blocks rendering until the resource is loaded.
correctAnswer: It tells the browser to fetch the resource early, reducing latency for critical assets.
explanation: Preload signals high priority, causing the browser to fetch the resource as soon as possible, improving perceived load time.

question: What is the purpose of resource hints like dns-prefetch, preconnect, and prefetch?
options: They reduce latency by resolving DNS, establishing connections, or fetching resources before they're needed.
They are used to hide resources from the user.
They are only for mobile devices.
They prevent caching.
correctAnswer: They reduce latency by resolving DNS, establishing connections, or fetching resources before they're needed.
explanation: These hints allow the browser to perform network optimizations ahead of time, lowering the cost of future requests.

question: How does the browser parse HTML incrementally, and what happens when it encounters a blocking script?
options: It parses and renders as it goes; a blocking script pauses parsing until the script is fetched and executed.
It waits until the entire document is loaded before parsing.
It ignores scripts entirely.
It parses scripts first, then the rest.
correctAnswer: It parses and renders as it goes; a blocking script pauses parsing until the script is fetched and executed.
explanation: Incremental parsing allows early rendering, but a blocking script halts parsing until it is downloaded and executed, delaying further parsing.

question: What is the difference between rel='preload' and rel='prefetch'?
options: preload loads resource immediately, prefetch loads when idle
preload loads when idle, prefetch loads immediately
preload is for CSS, prefetch is for JS
preload and prefetch are identical
correctAnswer: preload loads resource immediately, prefetch loads when idle
explanation: preload tells the browser to fetch a resource with high priority right away, while prefetch hints the browser to fetch it later when idle.

question: What are meta tags used for in SEO and social sharing (e.g., Open Graph tags)?
options: They define page layout
They provide metadata like title, description, image for search engines and social platforms
They control user authentication
They are used for styling
correctAnswer: They provide metadata like title, description, image for search engines and social platforms
explanation: Meta tags supply structured information that crawlers and social platforms use to display previews and index content.

question: What is the purpose of the robots meta tag?
options: To set the page's background color
To instruct search engine crawlers how to index or follow links
To enable JavaScript
To create navigation menus
correctAnswer: To instruct search engine crawlers how to index or follow links
explanation: The robots meta tag tells crawlers whether to index the page, follow links, or apply noindex/nofollow directives.

question: What is the difference between a canonical URL and a redirect for SEO purposes?
options: Canonical URL tells search engines the preferred URL; redirect changes the URL for users
Canonical URL redirects users; redirect tells search engines the preferred URL
Both are the same
Canonical URL is only for images
correctAnswer: Canonical URL tells search engines the preferred URL; redirect changes the URL for users
explanation: A canonical tag signals the preferred URL to search engines, while a redirect actually sends users and crawlers to a different URL.

question: What is structured data (schema.org / JSON-LD) and how does it help search engines?
options: It's a CSS framework
It's a way to embed machine-readable data to help search engines understand content
It's a JavaScript library for animations
It's a server-side language
correctAnswer: It's a way to embed machine-readable data to help search engines understand content
explanation: Structured data provides semantic context that search engines use to generate rich results and better understand page content.

question: What is the purpose of the sitemap and how does it relate to HTML/SEO?
options: It lists all pages for search engines to index, improving crawl efficiency.
It is a visual map of the website for users.
It contains CSS styles for navigation.
It is used to store user session data.
correctAnswer: It lists all pages for search engines to index, improving crawl efficiency.
explanation: A sitemap provides search engines with a structured list of URLs, helping them discover and index pages more efficiently, which directly supports SEO.

question: What is the difference between HTML validation and browser rendering leniency?
options: Validation checks syntax against the spec; browsers tolerate errors and still render.
Validation ensures accessibility; browsers ignore accessibility.
Validation is performed by search engines; browsers do not.
Validation is only for HTML5; browsers only support HTML4.
correctAnswer: Validation checks syntax against the spec; browsers tolerate errors and still render.
explanation: HTML validation enforces strict adherence to the specification, while browsers are designed to be forgiving and render pages even when markup is imperfect.

question: What is the difference between an HTML comment and a hidden element?
options: A comment is removed from the DOM; a hidden element remains in the DOM but is not displayed.
A comment is displayed to users; a hidden element is visible.
A comment is styled with CSS; a hidden element is not.
A comment is part of the CSS; a hidden element is part of the HTML.
correctAnswer: A comment is removed from the DOM; a hidden element remains in the DOM but is not displayed.
explanation: Comments are stripped from the DOM and never rendered, whereas hidden elements stay in the DOM tree but are not visible to the user.

question: What is the contenteditable attribute used for?
options: It makes an element's content editable by the user.
It hides the element from view.
It adds a tooltip to the element.
It defines the element's language.
correctAnswer: It makes an element's content editable by the user.
explanation: The contenteditable attribute turns an element into an editable region, allowing users to modify its text directly in the browser.

question: What is the difference between the <iframe> element and embedding content via Shadow DOM?
options: An iframe loads an entire separate document; Shadow DOM encapsulates part of the DOM with its own styles.
An iframe is used for images; Shadow DOM is used for text.
An iframe is a CSS feature; Shadow DOM is an HTML tag.
An iframe and Shadow DOM are identical in functionality.
correctAnswer: An iframe loads an entire separate document; Shadow DOM encapsulates part of the DOM with its own styles.
explanation: An iframe embeds a whole separate HTML document, while Shadow DOM creates a scoped subtree with isolated styles and markup within the same document.
